facts.fact_text: On 10 April 2006 a group of seven people living in the Dokuzparinskiy District of Dagestan posted a written notice informing the district authorities that on 25 April 2006 they would hold a public demonstration in the village of Usukhchay.
One of the principal aims of the demonstration planned for 25 April 2006 in the village of Usukhchay was to criticise the work of the head of the local administration, Mr A.
One of the principal aims of the demonstration planned for 25 April 2006 in the village of Usukhchay was to denounce corruption and the misuse of public funds by the local administration.

One of the principal aims of the demonstration planned for 25 April 2006 in the village of Usukhchay was to draw attention to the inactivity of the law-enforcement agencies regarding abuses committed by Mr A. and his colleagues.
The demonstration planned for 25 April 2006 was supposed to be held in a recreational park in the village of Usukhchay from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.
The estimated number of participants in the demonstration planned for 25 April 2006 in the village of Usukhchay was 5,000.
The first applicant took part in the "unauthorised" demonstration of 25 April 2006.
The third applicant took part in the "unauthorised" demonstration of 25 April 2006.

On 17 April 2006 the head of the district administration, Mr A. — the same person who was the principal target of the criticism by the demonstrators — informed the organisers that the district administration was opposed to the demonstration planned for 25 April 2006 in the village of Usukhchay.
In his letter of 17 April 2006, Mr A. stated that the notice of the demonstration had been lodged outside the time-limit fixed in the Public Gatherings Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004).
In his letter of 17 April 2006, Mr A. stated that the park in Usukhchay was not supposed to admit more than 500 people, making it impossible to hold the planned demonstration there.
Despite the decision of the local administration of 17 April 2006 whereby the demonstration of 25 April 2006 had not been allowed, the organisers decided to hold it as planned.
The first applicant took part in the "unauthorised" demonstration of 25 April 2006.
The third applicant took part in the "unauthorised" demonstration of 25 April 2006.

The second applicant was not amongst the protesters at the demonstration of 25 April 2006 because at that time he had been detained on remand in connection with the episode of 19 April 2006 in the village of Khiv.
At about 10 a.m. on 25 April 2006, a group of approximately 1,000 people gathered on the outskirts of Usukhchay.
Other demonstrators were unable to reach the assembly point on the outskirts of Usukhchay on 25 April 2006 because the roads had been blocked by the police.
The organisers of the demonstration on 25 April 2006 tried to meet representatives of the village administration in order to discuss the situation, but to no avail.
When the demonstrators started moving towards the centre of Usukhchay on 25 April 2006, the police blocked their way.
On 25 April 2006 another group of demonstrators from the neighbouring village of Miskindzha were stopped by the police on the way to Usukhchay.
The demonstrators from the village of Miskindzha were ordered by the police on 25 April 2006 to return to Miskindzha and hold their demonstration there separately, if they so wished.
In the afternoon of 25 April 2006, the demonstrators from Usukhchay started moving towards Miskindzha.
Because the police had blocked the road on 25 April 2006, the demonstrators moving from Usukhchay towards Miskindzha had to leave their cars and walk.
Because of bad weather and the long distance to walk, some demonstrators decided to give up on 25 April 2006 during the march from Usukhchay to Miskindzha.
When the demonstration arrived at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, there were no more than 200 to 300 participants.
The demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 was peaceful.
At about 3 p.m. on 25 April 2006, the demonstrators at Miskindzha were encircled by police officers from the Special Police Force Unit (OMON).
The police opened fire with automatic rifles above the demonstrators' heads at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
The police used tear gas to disperse the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
The police used smoke bombs to disperse the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
The police used stun grenades to disperse the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
The demonstrators at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 started to run in the direction of the village after the police opened fire and used special equipment.
The police officers followed the demonstrators running towards the village of Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 and beat them with rubber truncheons and rifle butts.
As a result of the dispersal of the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, one person was shot dead.
As a result of the dispersal of the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, five people were severely injured.

As a result of the dispersal of the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, several dozen people were beaten up or were injured by the shells of tear-gas bombs which had exploded in the midst of the crowd.
Sixty-seven people were arrested following the dispersal of the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
The organisers of the meeting of 25 April 2006 were charged in connection with their participation in the organisation of an unauthorised demonstration.

One of the participants in the demonstration of 25 April 2006, referring to the words of witness Mr S.F., claimed that the gunshot wound received by a police officer had been self-inflicted: the officer concerned had shot himself in the leg by accident because his gun had not been locked.
On 24 April 2006 the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Dagestan issued Order No. 7 "On measures to stabilise the situation in the Dokuzparinskiy District of Dagestan".

Order No. 7 of 24 April 2006 issued by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Dagestan described the unauthorised demonstration of 25 April 2006, which supposedly would involve about two thousand people "with an aggressive predisposition".

Order No. 7 of 24 April 2006 issued by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Dagestan mentioned the risks of blocking the roads and disturbing the normal work of State institutions in connection with the planned demonstration of 25 April 2006.

Order No. 7 of 24 April 2006 issued by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Dagestan provided for the formation of a "mixed squad" comprising thirty-five police officers from the Special Forces Unit of the Ministry (OMON) and 147 officers from eight local police stations.
Colonel Iz. was appointed as commander of the "mixed squad" formed pursuant to Order No. 7 of 24 April 2006 issued by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Dagestan.

Order No. 7 of 24 April 2006 issued by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Dagestan provided for undercover observation of the leaders of the demonstrators, video-recording of the events, strengthening of identity checks at the roadblocks and other security measures.

The "mixed squad" formed pursuant to Order No. 7 of 24 April 2006 moved to Usukhchay and took position at several roadblocks controlling roads leading to the village and near certain buildings occupied by State bodies.

The aim of the police operation in Usukhchay on 25 April 2006 was to secure public order, guarantee the constitutional rights and freedoms of the population and prevent clashes between the supporters of Mr A. and his opponents.
At about 11 a.m. on 25 April 2006, three groups of people gathered near the premises of the village administration in Usukhchay.
One group of about 150 people who gathered near the premises of the village administration in Usukhchay on 25 April 2006 were supporters of Mr A., the head of the district administration.
Two other groups — counting about one thousand people in aggregate — who gathered near the premises of the village administration in Usukhchay on 25 April 2006 were opponents of Mr A.

Official documents in the case file refer to another group of about 450 to 500 people who arrived in Usukhchay on 25 April 2006 to take part in the demonstration; it is unclear whether that group was able to join the gathering in the centre or was stopped by the police on the outskirts of the village.
In view of the risk of clashes between the opposing groups in Usukhchay on 25 April 2006, representatives of the protesters were invited to take part in negotiations in the local prosecutor's office.

The negotiations in the local prosecutor's office on 25 April 2006 involved Colonel Iz., the Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs of Dagestan, the prosecutor Ms Lg., and the head of the local police Mr Akb.
During the negotiations on 25 April 2006, the authorities proposed to the organisers of the demonstration that they could hold the demonstration in a municipal garage.
The offer to hold the demonstration in a municipal garage was declined by the demonstrators on 25 April 2006.
The demonstrators started to move from Usukhchay to Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, where they arrived at about 1 or 2 p.m.
Someone blocked the road connecting several villages near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 with objects including paving stones, timber beams and water pipes.
The blocked road near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 was a federal-level road connecting several villages, and its blockage caused a considerable traffic jam.

The authorities warned the organisers of the demonstration on 25 April 2006 that if the road near Miskindzha remained blocked, the organisers would be held liable and the law-enforcement authorities present on the spot would use force and "special equipment".
The organisers of the demonstration on 25 April 2006 refused to follow the instructions to unblock the road near Miskindzha and told other demonstrators to disobey the police orders.

When the police, following the orders of Deputy Minister Colonel Iz., started to remove the barricade from the road near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, unidentified men in the crowd started to throw stones at them.
Several shots were fired from a garden situated uphill on the left side of the road near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
Some of the protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 were armed with cold weapons such as iron rods, which they used as bats while attacking the police.
Some of the protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 tried to grab the service guns from the police officers.
As a result of the confrontation at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, the police used two stun grenades.
As a result of the confrontation at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, the police used twenty-three tear-gas grenades.
As a result of the confrontation at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, the police used thirty-six rubber bullets.
As a result of the confrontation at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, the police fired 747 shots from automatic rifles above the heads of the crowd.
Fifty-two of the most active protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 were arrested and taken to the Dokuzparinskiy police station.
Unidentified police officers used pump-action shotguns loaded with 22 mm grenades filled with tear gas at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, and those shots were fired in the direction of the crowd.
Following the clash between the police and the demonstrators at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, eleven police officers had bruises on their arms and legs, scratches and concussion.
Following the clash between the police and the demonstrators at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, one police officer had a ruptured spleen.
Following the clash between the police and the demonstrators at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, police officer Mr Il. had a gunshot wound in the form of a perforated bullet hole in the right thigh.
Following the clash at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, Mr Akh. had a blunt gunshot wound to the right side of the thorax with fractured ribs.
Following the clash at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, Mr Nsr. had a gunshot wound to the left side of the thorax with broken shoulder bones.
Following the clash at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, Mr Al. was wounded by a shell fragment in the right shin and thigh.
Following the clash at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, Mr Gnd. had a gunshot wound to the right forearm with a fractured bone.
Following the clash at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, Mr Ng. received a mortal wound by a gas grenade to the thorax and died on the way to hospital.
In support of their account of the events of 25 April 2006, the Government produced some documents apparently obtained in the course of the investigation (case no. 67610).
It is unclear whether all the documents produced by the Government related to case no. 67610 and whether they constituted the entirety of the materials collected within that case.
The Government produced medical certificates describing the injuries of several police officers following the clash at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, but not those of police officer Mr Il.
The Government produced several medical certificates describing the injuries sustained by the protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, all of whom had bruises and scratches.
According to the medical certificates, the protesters claimed that the police had kicked, beaten and battered them with rubber truncheons and gun butts during the events of 25 April 2006.
Some of the protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 had been injured by the rubber bullets used by the police.
Some protesters claimed that they had been beaten up after having been arrested and taken to the Dokuzparinskiy police station following the events of 25 April 2006.
Mr Akb., the head of the Dokuzparinskiy police, gave testimony about the events of 25 April 2006 that was generally consonant with the Government's account.
Mr Akb. stated that he had been warned about the demonstration of 25 April 2006 in a telegram sent by the organisers.
On 17 April 2006 Mr Akb. met one of the organisers of the demonstration and discussed the event.
At some time after 10 a.m. on 25 April 2006, Mr Akb.'s men stopped a large group of protesters who had been trying to enter Usukhchay.
Mr Akb. spoke with the leaders of the protesters on 25 April 2006 and explained to them that "the demonstration had not been authorised, and that the actions [of the demonstrators] were unlawful".

During negotiations on 25 April 2006, the deputy head of the district administration proposed to the protesters that they hold the demonstration in a municipal garage, explaining that if they stayed in the square near the district administration premises, they risked blocking the main road.
The leaders of the protesters visited the municipal garage on 25 April 2006 but were not satisfied with the offer to hold the demonstration there.
The leaders of the protesters informed the authorities on 25 April 2006 that they would send the protesters to Miskindzha and hold their demonstration there, in the village community centre.
After the negotiations on 25 April 2006, a small group of protesters started to move towards the village centre of Usukhchay, whereas others marched to Miskindzha, accompanied by the police.
At about 1 p.m. on 25 April 2006, Mr Akb. was informed that the federal road near Miskindzha had been blocked by two large heaps of stones.

Mr Akb. arrived at the scene near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 and started to negotiate with the leaders of the protesters, trying to persuade them to unblock the road, but they refused and insisted on meeting the leadership of the Dagestan Republic.
New people arrived at the scene near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, armed with stones and sticks.
Since the negotiations near Miskindzha had failed on 25 April 2006, Mr Akb. ordered the police to start clearing the road.

The men who had gathered on the sides of the road near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 started to throw stones at the police officers, several of whom were hit, so Mr Akb. authorised the use of shields and rubber truncheons.

Once the first heap of stones had been removed near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 and traffic had started to move, the police discovered that 300 metres further down the road it had again been obstructed with pipes.
Throughout the time the police were clearing the road near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, police officers had stones thrown at them.
Mr Akb. authorised the police to use firearms near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 but only above the heads of the protesters.
By 6 p.m. on 25 April 2006 the road near Miskindzha had been unblocked.
Witness Mr Yakh., one of the protesters, testified that when they had arrived in Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, the road had not yet been blocked.
Witness Mr Yakh. testified that people had started to block the road near Miskindzha spontaneously with stones in order to draw the authorities' attention to their claims.
Witness Mr Yakh. testified that the leaders of the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, who spoke before the crowd, called everybody to order and asked them not to break the law.
Witness Mr Yakh. testified that a police colonel appeared at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 and asked the leaders of the protesters to unblock the road, but they refused.

Witness Mr Yakh. testified that the police attacked the protesters from two sides at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 and started to shoot and throw gas grenades into the crowd, causing people to run in the direction of Miskindzha.

Witness Mr Yakh. testified that he had not seen protesters throwing stones at the police at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006; by contrast, the police had thrown stones at the crowd in order to unblock the road.

Witness Mr Ag., a district administration official, testified that all the protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, including women and elderly people, had been drunk, because earlier a mini-lorry had brought a cargo of vodka which had been distributed to the protesters.

Witness Mr Ag. testified that he joined the crowd and went with the protesters to Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, where he listened to the speeches of the leaders of the demonstration before a crowd of approximately 300 people.

Witness Mr Ag. testified that after the failure of the negotiations between the protesters and the authorities at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, the leaders started to incite the protesters to throw stones.
Witness Mr Ag. testified that he heard the sound of shots coming from the side where the protesters had gathered at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, and that a police officer was wounded.
Witness Mr Ag. testified that the police started to move towards the protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 and fired two or three warning shots above their heads.
Witness Mr Ag. testified that when the police started to remove the stones from the road and arrest the protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, he left.

Witness Mr Ag. testified that on the way back from Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 he overheard two women complaining that the organisers had not paid them and that they had been used as a human shield against the police.

According to an undated report by the head of the Special Forces Unit, Major Kr., the police had started using gas grenades at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 only when a large group of about 1,000 men armed with iron rods, wooden sticks and knives had attacked them.

Major Kr. specified in his undated report that when his officers were moving from the first barricade to the second near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, someone had started to shoot at them from under the nearby trees with an automatic gun and a hunter's gun.
Witness Mr Agb. testified that on 25 April 2006 he had been going on his business but had been stopped by the crowd near Miskindzha.
Witness Mr Agb. testified that he heard the first applicant calling the protesters not to block the road but to gather in the community centre of Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
Witness Mr Agb. testified that some of the demonstrators disobeyed the first applicant's call on 25 April 2006; two lorries arrived and dumped stones on the road near Miskindzha.
Witness Mr Agb. testified that some of the protesters were throwing stones at the police near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
Witness Mr Chub. was the driver of the lorry that had brought stones for the first barricade near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.

Witness Mr Chub. explained that he had loaded the stones near the river in order to build a shed in his garden, and that near the entry to Miskindzha he was stopped by a group of youngsters who ordered him, under the threat of violence, to dump the stones directly on the road.
The written testimonies of several other eyewitnesses of the events at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 were inconclusive.
Some eyewitnesses of the events at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 testified that a group of adolescents had been throwing stones at the police.
Some eyewitnesses of the events at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 testified that the police had used firearms by shooting in the air, whereas the demonstrators had no firearms.
Some eyewitnesses of the events at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 heard shots from the side of the protesters.
On 29 April 2006 the first applicant (Mr Primov) was arrested for participating in the organisation of an unauthorised demonstration on 25 April 2006 (criminal case no. 67610).

The first applicant (Mr Primov) was suspected of having committed a crime under Article 213 § 2 ("Hooliganism") of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation in connection with the events of 25 April 2006.

The first applicant (Mr Primov) was suspected of having committed a crime under Article 318 § 2 ("Use of violence against a public official") of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation in connection with the events of 25 April 2006.

The police suspected that the first applicant (Mr Primov) had incited the demonstrators to block the road and to "disobey the lawful orders of the police with the use of firearms" during the events of 25 April 2006.
The police applied to the Sovetskiy District Court of Makhachkala for a detention order against the first applicant (Mr Primov).

According to the Government, the decision of the Prosecutor of the Dagestan Republic (the Regional Prosecutor's Office) to seek the first applicant's (Mr Primov's) detention was based on the witness statements of Mr Als., Mr Agsh., Mr Shk. and an anonymous witness.

On 17 April 2006 the head of the district administration, Mr A. — the same person who was the principal target of the criticism by the demonstrators — informed the organisers that the district administration was opposed to the demonstration planned for 25 April 2006 in the village of Usukhchay.
In his letter of 17 April 2006, Mr A. stated that the notice of the demonstration had been lodged outside the time-limit fixed in the Public Gatherings Act (Federal Law no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004).
In his letter of 17 April 2006, Mr A. stated that the park in Usukhchay was not supposed to admit more than 500 people, making it impossible to hold the planned demonstration there.

The Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004, "the Public Gatherings Act") provided for the rights and duties of the organisers of public events as in force at the relevant time.

The relevant provisions of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) were summarised in detail in the case of Alekseyev v. Russia (nos. 4916/07, 25924/08 and 14599/09, § 50, 21 October 2010).

Section 5 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided that the organiser of a public event had to submit to the municipal authority a written notice in accordance with section 7 of that law.

Section 5 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided that the organiser had the right to hold a demonstration at the venue and time specified in the notice or as altered by agreement with the municipal authority.

Section 5 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided that the organiser had the right to hold assemblies at a venue that had been specially allocated or adapted to ensure the safety of citizens while such assemblies were held.

Section 5 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided that the organiser had to require the participants in the public event to observe public order and comply with the lawful requirements of the authorities.

Under section 5(5) of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), the organiser of the public event had no right to hold it if the notice on holding the public event had not been submitted in due time or no agreement had been reached with the municipal authorities on their reasoned proposal as to the alteration of the venue and/or time of the public event.

Section 7 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided that a written notice about a public event had to be lodged by the organiser with the municipal authority concerned not earlier than fifteen days and not later than ten days before the date of the event.

Under Part 2 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), the procedure for lodging notices of public events had to be defined in the regional legislation.

Under section 8 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), a public event could be held at any suitable venue provided that it did not threaten the safety of the participants.

Under section 12 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), the municipal authorities, upon receiving notice of the public event, had to propose an alternative venue and/or time for the public event if the original conditions set out in the notice did not correspond to the requirements of the law.

Under section 12 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), the municipal authorities also had to ensure, within their competence and jointly with the organisers and the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior, that public order and the safety of citizens while holding the event were respected.

Under section 19 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), decisions, acts or omissions of municipal authorities could be contested in court in accordance with the law.

New people arrived at the scene near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, armed with stones and sticks.
Since the negotiations near Miskindzha had failed on 25 April 2006, Mr Akb. ordered the police to start clearing the road.

The men who had gathered on the sides of the road near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 started to throw stones at the police officers, several of whom were hit, so Mr Akb. authorised the use of shields and rubber truncheons.

Once the first heap of stones had been removed near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 and traffic had started to move, the police discovered that 300 metres further down the road it had again been obstructed with pipes.
Throughout the time the police were clearing the road near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, police officers had stones thrown at them.
Mr Akb. authorised the police to use firearms near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 but only above the heads of the protesters.
By 6 p.m. on 25 April 2006 the road near Miskindzha had been unblocked.
Witness Mr Yakh., one of the protesters, testified that when they had arrived in Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, the road had not yet been blocked.
Witness Mr Yakh. testified that people had started to block the road near Miskindzha spontaneously with stones in order to draw the authorities' attention to their claims.
Witness Mr Yakh. testified that the leaders of the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, who spoke before the crowd, called everybody to order and asked them not to break the law.
Witness Mr Yakh. testified that a police colonel appeared at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 and asked the leaders of the protesters to unblock the road, but they refused.

Witness Mr Yakh. testified that the police attacked the protesters from two sides at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 and started to shoot and throw gas grenades into the crowd, causing people to run in the direction of Miskindzha.

Witness Mr Yakh. testified that he had not seen protesters throwing stones at the police at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006; by contrast, the police had thrown stones at the crowd in order to unblock the road.

Witness Mr Ag., a district administration official, testified that all the protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, including women and elderly people, had been drunk, because earlier a mini-lorry had brought a cargo of vodka which had been distributed to the protesters.

Witness Mr Ag. testified that he joined the crowd and went with the protesters to Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, where he listened to the speeches of the leaders of the demonstration before a crowd of approximately 300 people.

Witness Mr Ag. testified that after the failure of the negotiations between the protesters and the authorities at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, the leaders started to incite the protesters to throw stones.
Witness Mr Ag. testified that he heard the sound of shots coming from the side where the protesters had gathered at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, and that a police officer was wounded.
Witness Mr Ag. testified that the police started to move towards the protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 and fired two or three warning shots above their heads.
Witness Mr Ag. testified that when the police started to remove the stones from the road and arrest the protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, he left.

Witness Mr Ag. testified that on the way back from Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 he overheard two women complaining that the organisers had not paid them and that they had been used as a human shield against the police.

According to an undated report by the head of the Special Forces Unit, Major Kr., the police had started using gas grenades at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 only when a large group of about 1,000 men armed with iron rods, wooden sticks and knives had attacked them.

Major Kr. specified in his undated report that when his officers were moving from the first barricade to the second near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, someone had started to shoot at them from under the nearby trees with an automatic gun and a hunter's gun.
Witness Mr Agb. testified that on 25 April 2006 he had been going on his business but had been stopped by the crowd near Miskindzha.
Witness Mr Agb. testified that he heard the first applicant calling the protesters not to block the road but to gather in the community centre of Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
Witness Mr Agb. testified that some of the demonstrators disobeyed the first applicant's call on 25 April 2006; two lorries arrived and dumped stones on the road near Miskindzha.
Witness Mr Agb. testified that some of the protesters were throwing stones at the police near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
Witness Mr Chub. was the driver of the lorry that had brought stones for the first barricade near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.

Witness Mr Chub. explained that he had loaded the stones near the river in order to build a shed in his garden, and that near the entry to Miskindzha he was stopped by a group of youngsters who ordered him, under the threat of violence, to dump the stones directly on the road.
The written testimonies of several other eyewitnesses of the events at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 were inconclusive.
Some eyewitnesses of the events at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 testified that a group of adolescents had been throwing stones at the police.
Some eyewitnesses of the events at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 testified that the police had used firearms by shooting in the air, whereas the demonstrators had no firearms.
Some eyewitnesses of the events at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 heard shots from the side of the protesters.
At about 3 p.m. on 25 April 2006, the demonstrators at Miskindzha were encircled by police officers from the Special Police Force Unit (OMON).
The police opened fire with automatic rifles above the demonstrators' heads at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
The police used tear gas to disperse the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
The police used smoke bombs to disperse the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
The police used stun grenades to disperse the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
The demonstrators at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 started to run in the direction of the village after the police opened fire and used special equipment.
The police officers followed the demonstrators running towards the village of Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 and beat them with rubber truncheons and rifle butts.
As a result of the dispersal of the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, one person was shot dead.
As a result of the dispersal of the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, five people were severely injured.

As a result of the dispersal of the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, several dozen people were beaten up or were injured by the shells of tear-gas bombs which had exploded in the midst of the crowd.
Sixty-seven people were arrested following the dispersal of the demonstration at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
The organisers of the meeting of 25 April 2006 were charged in connection with their participation in the organisation of an unauthorised demonstration.
Several shots were fired from a garden situated uphill on the left side of the road near Miskindzha on 25 April 2006.
Some of the protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 were armed with cold weapons such as iron rods, which they used as bats while attacking the police.
Some of the protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 tried to grab the service guns from the police officers.
As a result of the confrontation at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, the police used two stun grenades.
As a result of the confrontation at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, the police used twenty-three tear-gas grenades.
As a result of the confrontation at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, the police used thirty-six rubber bullets.
As a result of the confrontation at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, the police fired 747 shots from automatic rifles above the heads of the crowd.
Fifty-two of the most active protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 were arrested and taken to the Dokuzparinskiy police station.
Unidentified police officers used pump-action shotguns loaded with 22 mm grenades filled with tear gas at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, and those shots were fired in the direction of the crowd.
Following the clash between the police and the demonstrators at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, eleven police officers had bruises on their arms and legs, scratches and concussion.
Following the clash between the police and the demonstrators at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, one police officer had a ruptured spleen.
Following the clash between the police and the demonstrators at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, police officer Mr Il. had a gunshot wound in the form of a perforated bullet hole in the right thigh.
Following the clash at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, Mr Akh. had a blunt gunshot wound to the right side of the thorax with fractured ribs.
Following the clash at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, Mr Nsr. had a gunshot wound to the left side of the thorax with broken shoulder bones.
Following the clash at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, Mr Al. was wounded by a shell fragment in the right shin and thigh.
Following the clash at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, Mr Gnd. had a gunshot wound to the right forearm with a fractured bone.
Following the clash at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, Mr Ng. received a mortal wound by a gas grenade to the thorax and died on the way to hospital.
In support of their account of the events of 25 April 2006, the Government produced some documents apparently obtained in the course of the investigation (case no. 67610).
It is unclear whether all the documents produced by the Government related to case no. 67610 and whether they constituted the entirety of the materials collected within that case.
The Government produced medical certificates describing the injuries of several police officers following the clash at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, but not those of police officer Mr Il.
The Government produced several medical certificates describing the injuries sustained by the protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006, all of whom had bruises and scratches.
According to the medical certificates, the protesters claimed that the police had kicked, beaten and battered them with rubber truncheons and gun butts during the events of 25 April 2006.
Some of the protesters at Miskindzha on 25 April 2006 had been injured by the rubber bullets used by the police.
Some protesters claimed that they had been beaten up after having been arrested and taken to the Dokuzparinskiy police station following the events of 25 April 2006.

Article 30 of the Constitution of the Russian Federation provides that everyone has the right to freedom of association.

Article 55 § 3 of the Constitution of the Russian Federation provides that rights and freedoms may be restricted by federal laws for the protection of constitutional principles, public morals, health and the rights and lawful interests of others, and to ensure the defence and security of the State.

The Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004, "the Public Gatherings Act") provided for the rights and duties of the organisers of public events as in force at the relevant time.

The relevant provisions of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) were summarised in detail in the case of Alekseyev v. Russia (nos. 4916/07, 25924/08 and 14599/09, § 50, 21 October 2010).

Section 5 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided that the organiser of a public event had to submit to the municipal authority a written notice in accordance with section 7 of that law.

Section 5 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided that the organiser had the right to hold a demonstration at the venue and time specified in the notice or as altered by agreement with the municipal authority.

Section 5 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided that the organiser had the right to hold assemblies at a venue that had been specially allocated or adapted to ensure the safety of citizens while such assemblies were held.

Section 5 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided that the organiser had to require the participants in the public event to observe public order and comply with the lawful requirements of the authorities.

Under section 5(5) of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), the organiser of the public event had no right to hold it if the notice on holding the public event had not been submitted in due time or no agreement had been reached with the municipal authorities on their reasoned proposal as to the alteration of the venue and/or time of the public event.

Section 7 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided that a written notice about a public event had to be lodged by the organiser with the municipal authority concerned not earlier than fifteen days and not later than ten days before the date of the event.

Under Part 2 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), the procedure for lodging notices of public events had to be defined in the regional legislation.

Under section 8 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), a public event could be held at any suitable venue provided that it did not threaten the safety of the participants.

Under section 12 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), the municipal authorities, upon receiving notice of the public event, had to propose an alternative venue and/or time for the public event if the original conditions set out in the notice did not correspond to the requirements of the law.

Under section 12 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), the municipal authorities also had to ensure, within their competence and jointly with the organisers and the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior, that public order and the safety of citizens while holding the event were respected.

Under section 19 of the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), decisions, acts or omissions of municipal authorities could be contested in court in accordance with the law.

Under the Code of Civil Procedure of 2002, a person affected by an unlawful administrative act or omission by a State or municipal authority disposes of two types of remedy: a "complaint" or a "claim" (иск) against the State.
Complaints under the Code of Civil Procedure of 2002 are governed by Chapter 25 of the Code ("Challenging decisions, acts or omissions of State and municipal authorities and officials").
The Code of Civil Procedure of 2002 provides for judicial review of decisions and other acts of State or municipal officials if those acts breached the rights and freedoms of the interested person.

Article 258 § 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure of 2002 provides that a complaint must not be granted if the action challenged in court "is in compliance with the law, has been taken within the jurisdiction of the State body or official and the rights and freedoms of the citizen have not been violated".

As follows from Article 258 of the Code of Civil Procedure of 2002, a successful plaintiff under Chapter 25 may obtain an injunction against the State body or official concerned, by which the court must require "full elimination of the breach of the rights and freedoms".
The Code of Civil Procedure of 2002 is silent on whether Chapter 25 allows the plaintiff to seek reliefs other than an injunction, in particular damages.
Article 257 of the Code of Civil Procedure of 2002 provides that complaints lodged under Chapter 25 of the Code must be examined within ten days from the date of their lodging.
Under Article 338 of the Code of Civil Procedure of 2002, the parties have ten days to lodge an appeal following a decision on a complaint under Chapter 25.
Under Article 348 of the Code of Civil Procedure of 2002, the Court of Appeal has one month from the date of its receipt to consider an appeal lodged under Article 338.
